title: Scaling and RevShare
summary: How RevShare really pays, how negative carryover changes your cash flow, and when to choose CPA, RevShare or hybrid as you grow. You will build a portfolio of licensed partners, support retention honestly and negotiate better deals with data before scaling within caps.

lessons.title: RevShare maths in depth
objectives: By the end you can calculate GGR, NGR and your RevShare commission from an operator statement.
By the end you can compare deals with different percentages, admin fees and tier rules.
By the end you can list the contract terms that decide what a RevShare deal is really worth.

steps.h: Why the small print is the deal
steps.p: Two RevShare offers with the same headline percentage can pay very different amounts. What counts as revenue, what is deducted first, how tiers work and how long you are paid all sit in the contract. Read it before you send a single player, because you cannot renegotiate players already sent.

d.b: The percentage is the headline, not the deal
d.s: Definitions decide what you are paid.

steps.say: Here's something many affiliates learn too late. Two RevShare offers with the same headline percentage can pay very different amounts. What counts as revenue, what's deducted first, how tiers work, and how long you're paid, all of that sits in the contract. As the screen says, the percentage is the headline, not the deal. Read it before you send a single player, because you can't renegotiate players already sent.

steps.p: GGR (gross gaming revenue) is what players staked minus what they won. NGR (net gaming revenue) is GGR minus deductions the contract allows, usually bonuses and often fees or taxes. Your RevShare percentage applies to NGR.
d: GGR
Bonuses and allowed deductions
NGR
steps.say: Let's define the terms. G G R, gross gaming revenue, is what players staked minus what they won. N G R, net gaming revenue, is G G R minus the deductions the contract allows, usually bonuses, and often fees or taxes. Look at the formula on screen: G G R, minus bonuses and allowed deductions, equals N G R. And your RevShare percentage applies to N G R, not G G R.

steps.p: Example: an operator statement for your players in one month. Follow each line down to your commission. The deductions shown are common, but your contract decides which ones apply.
steps.say: Here's an example statement for one month. Follow each line down. Players staked fifty thousand dollars, and forty five thousand five hundred was paid back in winnings. So G G R is four thousand five hundred. Bonuses take nine hundred, and fees and taxes take six hundred. That leaves N G R of three thousand. Your thirty percent share is nine hundred dollars. These deductions are common, but your contract decides which ones apply.

steps.h: From a player's bet to your payment
steps.p: Every RevShare payment follows the same chain. When a number on your statement looks wrong, walk back along this chain to find the step where your figure and the operator's differ.
d: Stakes
Minus winnings = GGR
Minus deductions = NGR
× your share
Invoice
Payment
steps.say: Every RevShare payment follows this same chain. Look at the flow. Stakes, minus winnings gives G G R. Minus deductions gives N G R. Times your share. Then an invoice, then payment. Why does this matter? When a number on your statement looks wrong, walk back along this chain to find the exact step where your figure and the operator's differ.

steps.p: Example: two offers on the same player activity, GGR of $10,000 after bonuses. Offer A pays a higher percentage but takes a 20% admin fee first. Offer B pays less but deducts nothing extra. The lower headline pays more.
steps.more: Always convert every offer into the same test: 'what do I earn on $10,000 of GGR after bonuses?' Ask the operator for a sample statement so you can see the real deductions. If they will not show one, treat that as a warning sign.
steps.say: Admin fees change everything. In this example, two offers on the same activity, ten thousand dollars of G G R after bonuses. Offer A pays thirty five percent, but takes a twenty percent admin fee first. So it's eight thousand times thirty five percent, two thousand eight hundred dollars. Offer B pays thirty percent with no admin fee, three thousand dollars. The lower headline pays more. Always compare offers on the same ten thousand dollars, and ask for a sample statement. If they won't show one, treat that as a warning sign.

steps.h: What a monthly statement looks like
steps.p: Example of a statement screen. Layouts differ, but the same lines appear. Check each deduction against your contract, and keep a copy of every statement with your deal sheet.
steps.say: Here's an example statement screen. Layouts differ, but you'll see the same lines. G G R, four thousand five hundred. Bonuses, minus nine hundred. Fees and taxes, minus six hundred. N G R, three thousand. And commission at thirty percent, nine hundred. Check each deduction against your contract, and keep a copy of every statement with your deal sheet.

steps.p: Many deals raise the percentage as your monthly NGR grows. The contract says whether the higher rate applies to all your NGR or only to the part above each threshold. On the same month the difference is real money. Example tiers: 25% up to $5,000 of NGR, 30% from there to $15,000.
steps.more: Check: $5,000 × 25% = $1,250. $7,000 × 30% = $2,100. $1,250 + $2,100 = $3,350. Whole-amount tiers pay $250 more this month. Neither is wrong; you just need to know which one you are signing so your forecasts are right.
steps.say: Many deals raise your percentage as monthly N G R grows. The contract says whether the higher rate applies to all your N G R, or only to the part above each threshold. In this example, tiers are twenty five percent up to five thousand, and thirty percent from there to fifteen thousand. On twelve thousand dollars of N G R, the whole-amount basis pays three thousand six hundred. The marginal basis pays three thousand three hundred and fifty. Neither is wrong, but you need to know which you're signing.

steps.p: Before accepting any RevShare or hybrid deal, find these clauses and copy them into your deal sheet. If a clause is missing or vague, ask in writing.
d: NGR definition|exactly what is deducted from GGR
Admin fee|any percentage taken before your share
Negative carryover|whether losses roll into next month
Duration|lifetime of the player or a fixed period
Tier basis|whole amount or marginal bands
Changes clause|how and with what notice terms can change
steps.say: Before accepting any RevShare or hybrid deal, find these six clauses. The N G R definition, exactly what's deducted from G G R. The admin fee, any percentage taken before your share. Negative carryover, whether losses roll into next month. Duration, lifetime of the player or a fixed period. Tier basis, whole amount or marginal bands. And the changes clause, how and with what notice terms can change. Copy them into your deal sheet, and if a clause is missing or vague, ask in writing.

steps.p: Walk through the contract in this order. It takes twenty minutes and stops most surprises. Clause names differ; search for the words shown. Copy what you find straight into your deal sheet.

steps.title: Find the NGR definition
steps.text: Search 'net gaming revenue' or 'net revenue'. List every deduction.

blocks.value: NGR means GGR less bonuses, payment processing fees, gaming taxes and an administration fee of 15%.

steps.title: Find carryover
steps.text: Search 'negative', 'carry' or 'carried forward'.

blocks.value: Negative NGR in any month shall be carried forward and offset against future positive NGR.

steps.title: Find duration and tiers
steps.text: Search 'lifetime', 'months', 'tier'.

steps.title: Find the changes clause
steps.text: Search 'amend' or 'change'. Note the notice period.

blocks.value: Company may amend commission terms with 14 days notice by email.

blocks.label: Your note
blocks.value: Ask: do changes apply to players already referred?

steps.title: Fill your deal sheet
steps.text: One row per deal so you can compare like for like.

steps.say: Let's read a contract. Tap Next to follow each step. First, find the N G R definition: search net gaming revenue, and list every deduction. Here, there's a fifteen percent admin fee. Second, find carryover: search negative, carry or carried forward. Third, find duration and tiers. Here it's lifetime of the player, with whole-amount tiers. Fourth, find the changes clause and note the notice period. Here, fourteen days by email, so ask whether changes apply to players already referred. It takes about twenty minutes.

steps.p: These are the mistakes that make a 'good' RevShare deal pay far less than the affiliate expected. Each fix takes a few minutes before signing and can be worth hundreds of dollars a month after.

a.title: Mistake
items: Assuming lifetime when it is 12 months
Accepting changes by email without reading

b.title: Fix
items: Value only inside the paid period
Ask if changes hit existing players

steps.say: These mistakes make a good-looking deal pay far less than expected. Comparing headline percentages only. Ignoring the admin fee. Assuming lifetime when it's twelve months. Not knowing the tier basis. And accepting changes by email without reading. The fixes: compare on ten thousand dollars of G G R, ask for a sample statement, value only inside the paid period, model both tier bases, and ask if changes hit existing players.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. They make every deal comparable and stop you from signing on a headline. Apply them to every new offer, including ones a friend or a forum recommends.
d: Compare every deal on commission per $10,000 GGR after bonuses
No sample statement: treat the deal as higher risk
Fixed-period deals: count value only inside the period
Changes clause with no protection for existing players: negotiate or prefer another deal
Write every term into your deal sheet before sending traffic
steps.say: Here are starting decision rules to adapt. Compare every deal on commission per ten thousand dollars of G G R after bonuses. No sample statement, treat the deal as higher risk. Fixed-period deals, count value only inside the period. A changes clause with no protection for existing players, negotiate or prefer another deal. And write every term into your deal sheet before sending traffic. Apply these to every offer, even ones a friend or forum recommends.

steps.p: On RevShare your income rises when your players lose more. That makes it more important, not less, to market honestly and never encourage chasing losses, longer play or bigger deposits. Some regulators restrict revenue-share deals for affiliates for exactly this reason.

d.text: Some jurisdictions restrict or ban revenue-share affiliate deals. Check local law in each geo and your platform's gambling policy. We are not certain this is current; check your contract and the operator's terms before relying on it.

steps.h: Read once, earn correctly for years
steps.p: A lifetime RevShare deal can pay you for years on players you sent this month. That is the upside. The same contract terms apply for all those years, which is why twenty minutes of reading now matters more than any creative test.

d.b: The contract runs as long as the players do
d.s: Read it before the first player.

steps.say: A lifetime RevShare deal can pay you for years on players you sent this month. That's the upside. But the same contract terms apply for all those years. That's why twenty minutes of reading now matters more than any creative test. As the screen says, the contract runs as long as the players do. Read it before the first player.

takeaways: Your share applies to NGR, and the contract defines NGR.
Compare deals on commission per $10,000 of GGR after bonuses.
Admin fees, tier basis, duration and changes clauses can outweigh the headline percentage.
RevShare ties your income to player losses; market more carefully, not less.

lessons.title: Negative carryover, month by month
objectives: By the end you can calculate RevShare commission with and without negative carryover over several months.
By the end you can track a carried balance and forecast when it clears.
By the end you can apply rules that protect your cash flow from big player wins.

steps.h: Why one winner can cost you months
steps.p: When a player wins big, NGR for that month can go negative. With negative carryover, that negative amount is subtracted from your future months until it is used up. One lucky player can wipe out commission you were counting on for two or three months.

d.b: A big win is carried into your future
d.s: Know the rule before the winner arrives.

steps.say: When a player wins big, N G R, net gaming revenue, for that month can go negative. With negative carryover, that negative amount is subtracted from your future months until it's used up. So one lucky player can wipe out commission you were counting on for two or three months. As the screen says, know the rule before the winner arrives.

steps.p: Each month, add the carried balance to this month's NGR. If the total is positive, you are paid your share and the balance resets to zero. If it is negative, you are paid nothing and the negative total carries forward.
d: This month's NGR
Carried balance
Commission base (paid only if > 0)
steps.say: Here's the carryover formula. Each month, add the carried balance to this month's N G R. That gives your commission base. If the total is positive, you're paid your share and the balance resets to zero. If it's negative, you're paid nothing, and the negative total carries forward into next month.

steps.p: Example: 30% RevShare. In month 2 a player wins big and NGR is −$5,000. Watch how it eats into months 3 and 4. Follow the 'base after carry' column; it is the number your share is calculated on.
steps.more: Month 3: −$5,000 + $4,000 = −$1,000, still negative, so nothing is paid and −$1,000 carries. Month 4: −$1,000 + $3,000 = +$2,000. $2,000 × 30% = $600. Over four months the players produced $5,000 of NGR in total (3,000 − 5,000 + 4,000 + 3,000) and 30% of $5,000 is exactly the $1,500 you were paid.
steps.say: Let's walk through an example at thirty percent RevShare. Month one, N G R is three thousand, so you're paid nine hundred. Month two, a player wins big, N G R is minus five thousand, so you're paid nothing and carry minus five thousand. Month three, N G R is four thousand, but after the carry, the base is still minus one thousand, so nothing again. Month four, three thousand plus minus one thousand gives two thousand, so you're paid six hundred. Total, fifteen hundred dollars.

steps.p: Same players, same months, but the deal resets negative months to zero. The negative month pays nothing, but it does not reduce later months. Compare the total at the bottom with the previous slide.
steps.more: The difference is $3,000 − $1,500 = $1,500 over four months, from one clause. With carryover you are paid on true net results. Without it, the operator absorbs the losing month. That is why operators prefer carryover and why removing it is one of the most valuable things to negotiate once you have volume.
steps.say: Now the same players and months, but this deal resets negative months to zero. Month one pays nine hundred. Month two pays nothing, but it doesn't reduce later months. Month three pays twelve hundred on four thousand. Month four pays nine hundred. Total, three thousand dollars. Compare that with fifteen hundred on the previous slide. That difference comes from one clause, and it's why removing carryover is valuable to negotiate once you have volume.

steps.h: Example: cumulative commission over seven months
steps.p: Example: the same players continue at +$2,500, +$2,000 and +$2,000 in months 5 to 7. The no-carryover line pulls ahead in month 3 and stays $1,500 ahead.
steps.say: Look at these two lines. It's an example of cumulative commission over seven months, with the same players continuing at two thousand five hundred, two thousand and two thousand in months five to seven. The no-carryover line pulls ahead in month three, and stays fifteen hundred dollars ahead all the way to month seven.

steps.p: Example: over four months the same players paid $3,000 without carryover and $1,500 with it. One clause halved the commission in this case. On a bigger account the same clause can be worth thousands a month.

d.label: difference over four months
d.note: Example from the previous two slides.

steps.say: Here's the cost of one clause. In this example, over four months, the same players paid three thousand dollars without carryover, and fifteen hundred with it. The difference is fifteen hundred dollars, the number on screen. One clause halved the commission in this case. And on a bigger account, the same clause can be worth thousands a month.

steps.p: Carryover is not one rule. Read exactly which version you have, because each one behaves differently when a big win lands. Ask your manager which one applies, and get the answer in writing.
d: Pooled|negatives across all brands offset each other
Per brand|each brand's negative stays with that brand
Rolling|carries until it is used up, however long
Capped or time-limited|resets after a set period or amount
None|each month stands alone
steps.say: Carryover isn't one rule. Look at the cards. Pooled, where negatives across all brands offset each other. Per brand, where each brand's negative stays with that brand. Rolling, which carries until it's used up, however long. Capped or time-limited, which resets after a set period or amount. And none, where each month stands alone. Ask your manager which version applies to you, and get the answer in writing.

steps.p: Keep your own carryover ledger. Operator dashboards do not always show the balance clearly, and you need it for cash forecasts. A spreadsheet with three formulas is enough.

steps.title: One row per month per deal
steps.text: Record NGR exactly as the statement shows it.

steps.title: Add the formula
steps.text: Base = NGR + carry in. Paid = 30% of base if positive. Carry out = base if negative, else zero.

steps.title: Check against the statement
steps.text: Your paid amount should match the operator's. If not, ask which deductions differ.

steps.title: Forecast the clear date
steps.text: Divide the carried negative by your average monthly NGR to estimate months to clear.

steps.say: Keep your own carryover ledger, because operator dashboards don't always show the balance clearly. Tap Next to follow each step. First, one row per month per deal, recording N G R exactly as the statement shows. Second, add the formulas on screen: base, paid, and carry out. Third, check your paid amount against the operator's statement, and if it differs, ask which deductions differ. Fourth, forecast the clear date: here, minus five thousand divided by three thousand average N G R is about one point seven months.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. They stop one player's luck from breaking your cash flow or your budget plan. Write them next to your carryover ledger so you see them every month.
steps.more: Example: average commission $900 a month, so two months is $1,800. A carried balance of −$5,000 NGR equals $1,500 of lost commission at 30%, just under the line. A −$7,000 balance ($2,100) would pass it, and that is the moment to talk to your manager with your ledger.
d: Budget ad spend from cash received, never from expected RevShare
One player > 25% of monthly NGR: expect swings, do not plan on that month
Carried negative > 2 months of average commission: ask for a reset or shift new volume to CPA or hybrid
Prefer per-brand over pooled carryover when you run several brands
Once you have 3 months of steady volume, ask to remove carryover
steps.say: Here are starting carryover rules to adapt. Budget ad spend from cash received, never from expected RevShare. If one player is over twenty five percent of monthly N G R, expect swings and don't plan on that month. If the carried negative is over two months of average commission, ask for a reset, or shift new volume to C P A, cost per acquisition, or hybrid. Prefer per-brand over pooled carryover. And once you have three months of steady volume, ask to remove carryover.

steps.p: Here is how to raise a large carried balance with your manager. Lead with the ledger, explain the cause, and make a specific request. The answer may be no; ask anyway once you have steady volume.

messages.text: One player's win in March left a carried balance of −$7,000. Our other players are steady: 3 months above $3,000 NGR. Ledger attached.
Could you reset the balance, or move new players to per-brand carryover?
I can't reset March, but new players from next month go on per-brand carryover. I'll confirm by email.

steps.say: In this chat, the affiliate raises a large carried balance. Notice how. They lead with the facts: one player's win in March left minus seven thousand, and other players are steady, three months above three thousand N G R, with the ledger attached. Then a specific request: reset the balance, or move new players to per-brand carryover. The manager can't reset March, but agrees per-brand for new players, and will confirm by email. The answer may be no, but ask anyway once you have steady volume.

steps.p: These mistakes turn a normal swing into a cash crisis. Each one has a fix that costs nothing but discipline. Check yourself against the left column every quarter.

a.title: Mistake
items: Spending next month's RevShare before it arrives
Not knowing carryover exists until month 3
Pooling all brands under one negative
Panic-cutting good traffic after one big win

b.title: Fix
items: Read the clause before the first player
Judge traffic on cohort value, not one month

steps.say: These mistakes turn a normal swing into a cash crisis. Spending next month's RevShare before it arrives. Not knowing carryover exists until month three. Pooling all brands under one negative. And panic-cutting good traffic after one big win. The fixes: spend only cash received, read the clause before the first player, ask for per-brand carryover, and judge traffic on cohort value, not one month.

steps.p: Carryover rules differ by operator, by network and sometimes by deal. Some operators have dropped carryover; others keep it strictly. Do not assume what you read here or elsewhere applies to your contract.

steps.h: A player's win is not your loss to fix
steps.p: When a player wins, that is the game working as advertised. Never respond by trying to win the money back through more aggressive marketing to that player or anyone else. Carryover is a business risk you manage with contracts and cash, not with pressure.

d.b: Manage carryover with contracts and cash

steps.say: When a player wins, that's the game working as advertised. Never respond by trying to win that money back through more aggressive marketing, to that player or anyone else. Carryover is a business risk. As the screen says, you manage it with contracts and cash, never with pressure on players.

takeaways: With carryover, a negative month is subtracted from later months until it clears.
Over time you are paid your share of true net NGR; without carryover you keep more.
Keep your own ledger and forecast when a balance clears.
Spend only cash received, and negotiate carryover once you have volume.

lessons.title: CPA, RevShare or hybrid at scale
objectives: By the end you can model the same cohort under CPA, RevShare and hybrid deals.
By the end you can find the payback month for each deal type.
By the end you can decide with a rule when to move part of your volume to RevShare or hybrid.

steps.h: Why deal type is a cash decision
steps.p: CPA pays soon after the player qualifies. RevShare pays slowly, over months or years. Hybrid sits between. The same players can make you profitable this month or leave you short of cash for half a year, depending only on the deal type.

d.s: Choose the deal your bank account can carry.

steps.say: C P A, cost per acquisition, pays soon after the player qualifies. RevShare pays slowly, over months or years. Hybrid sits in between. So the same players can make you profitable this month, or leave you short of cash for half a year, depending only on the deal type. As the screen says, choose the deal your bank account can carry.

steps.h: Worked example: one cohort, three deals
steps.p: Example: 100 qualified players acquired for $3,000, so $30 each. Six-month NGR for the cohort is $6,000, the figure from Module 5. Compare what each deal pays by month six.
steps.more: At these numbers CPA wins by month six. RevShare only catches up if players keep generating NGR for much longer. To reach the $4,000 CPA total at 30%, the cohort would need $13,333 of NGR, more than twice its six-month figure. That can happen with long-lived players, which is why some affiliates hold RevShare as a long-term asset, but it is never guaranteed.
steps.say: Here's an example cohort: one hundred qualified players, acquired for three thousand dollars, thirty each. Six-month N G R, net gaming revenue, is six thousand. Look at the table. C P A at forty dollars pays four thousand, a thousand profit. RevShare at thirty percent pays eighteen hundred, a twelve hundred loss so far. Hybrid at twenty dollars plus twenty percent pays thirty two hundred, two hundred profit. At these numbers C P A wins by month six. RevShare only catches up if players keep playing much longer, and that's never guaranteed.

steps.p: Example: the same cohort's commission by month six under each deal, as bars. CPA is the longest bar here, but that depends entirely on how long players stay and on the percentages offered.

Hybrid $20 + 20%

steps.say: These bars show the same comparison. It's the example cohort's commission by month six under each deal. C P A is the longest bar here, at four thousand dollars. Hybrid follows at thirty two hundred, and RevShare at eighteen hundred. But remember, that ranking depends entirely on how long players stay, and on the percentages offered.

steps.p: Example: cumulative commission per deal for the cohort above. CPA pays almost at once. RevShare climbs slowly and flattens as players leave. The gap is the price of waiting.

steps.p: Payback is the first month when cumulative commission is at least what you spent to acquire the cohort. Before it, the cohort is a loan you made. After it, every payment is profit.
steps.more: Example: spend $3,000. Hybrid cumulative: month 1 $2,000 + 20% × $2,500 = $2,500; month 2 $2,000 + 20% × $3,700 = $2,740; month 3 $2,900; month 4 $3,020. Payback is month 4. RevShare at 30% reaches only $1,890 by month 7, so no payback in the period shown.

Acquisition spend
Payback month
steps.say: Payback is the first month when cumulative commission is at least what you spent to acquire the cohort. Before that month, the cohort is like a loan you made. After it, every payment is profit. In this example, spend is three thousand. The hybrid deal reaches three thousand and twenty in month four, so payback is month four. RevShare at thirty percent reaches only eighteen ninety by month seven, so there's no payback in the period shown.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. They let you take long-term upside without risking the cash that keeps your campaigns running. Write the numbers for each partner in your deal sheet.
steps.more: Example: 6-month value $60 per player at 35% RevShare = $21. CPA × 1.2 = $40 × 1.2 = $48. $21 is far below $48, so stay on CPA. If six-month value were $150, 35% gives $52.50, above $48, and a RevShare test would make sense.

steps.say: Here are starting deal-type rules to adapt. In a new geo or source, use C P A first, until you have ninety-day cohort data. Move volume to RevShare only if six-month value times the RevShare percent beats C P A times one point two. Never fund RevShare with cash you need within six months. Use hybrid when the operator won't raise C P A but you want some upside. And cap RevShare acquisition at a set share of monthly spend, for example twenty percent.

steps.h: Cash you need to carry RevShare
steps.p: Example: if you acquire $3,000 of players a month on RevShare and a cohort pays back slowly, your cash is tied up month after month. Work out how much before you start.
steps.more: Received each month is the sum of every cohort's RevShare that month. Month 1: cohort 1 pays $750. Month 2: cohort 1 pays $360 more (cumulative $1,110) and cohort 2 pays $750, so cumulative received is $750 + $360 + $750 = $1,860. Month 3: cohort 1 +$240, cohort 2 +$360, cohort 3 +$750 = $1,350, cumulative $3,210. Cash tied up keeps growing for months. That is why the rules cap the RevShare share of spend.
steps.say: How much cash do you need to carry RevShare? In this example, you acquire three thousand dollars of players a month. By month one, you've spent three thousand and received seven fifty, so twenty two fifty is tied up. By month two, six thousand spent, eighteen sixty received, forty one forty tied up. By month three, nine thousand spent, thirty two ten received, fifty seven ninety tied up. Cash tied up keeps growing for months. That's why the rules cap RevShare's share of spend.

steps.p: Most deal-type mistakes come from choosing the long-term deal without the cash to wait for it. Each fix keeps your cash safe while you build the long-term side.

steps.say: Most deal-type mistakes come from choosing the long-term deal without the cash to wait for it. RevShare on a brand new source. Funding RevShare from next month's ad budget. Compare at six months or later. And mix, mostly C P A with a capped RevShare share.

lessons.title: Building a portfolio of operators, geos and products
objectives: By the end you can measure concentration risk in your revenue.
By the end you can run due diligence on a new operator before sending volume.
By the end you can plan a portfolio that spreads risk across operators, geos and products.

steps.h: Why one operator is a single point of failure
steps.p: Operators lose licences, leave markets, change terms, delay payments and close affiliate programmes. If one operator is most of your revenue, any of those events can stop your business overnight. A portfolio does not raise your best month; it protects you from your worst.

d.b: Spread the risk before you need to
d.s: A portfolio protects your worst month.

steps.say: Operators lose licences, leave markets, change terms, delay payments, and close affiliate programmes. If one operator is most of your revenue, any of those events can stop your business overnight. A portfolio doesn't raise your best month. As the screen says, it protects your worst month. So spread the risk before you need to.

steps.h: What can go wrong with one partner
steps.p: These events happen in iGaming every year. None of them is a sign you did anything wrong, and all of them hurt more when one partner is most of your income.
d: Licence loss or market exit|traffic stops paying at once
Term changes|lower CPA or new carryover rules
Payment delays|cash flow breaks while spend continues
Cap cuts|volume above the cap may not be paid
Programme closure|lifetime RevShare can end
steps.say: Look at these cards. They're events that happen in iGaming every year. Licence loss or market exit, where traffic stops paying at once. Term changes, like a lower C P A, cost per acquisition, or new carryover rules. Payment delays, where cash flow breaks while spend continues. Cap cuts, where volume above the cap may not be paid. And programme closure, where lifetime RevShare can end. None of these means you did anything wrong, but all of them hurt more when one partner is most of your income.

steps.p: Concentration is the share of your monthly commission that comes from your largest partner. It is the simplest measure of how exposed you are. Work it out every month from your commission statements.
steps.more: Example: total monthly commission $10,000. Operator A pays $6,000. Concentration = $6,000 ÷ $10,000 = 60%. If A stopped paying, you would lose 60% of income while your ad spend commitments continued for days or weeks.
d: Largest partner's commission
Total commission
Concentration
steps.say: Concentration is the share of your monthly commission that comes from your largest partner. The formula is your largest partner's commission divided by total commission. In this example, total commission is ten thousand dollars, and operator A pays six thousand. So concentration is sixty percent. If A stopped paying, you'd lose sixty percent of income while ad spend commitments continued. Work this out every month from your statements.

steps.p: Example: a plan to bring concentration under 40% over a few months by growing other partners, not by cutting the one that works. Read the 'Target' column as a direction, not a deadline.
steps.more: A stays the same in dollars but drops to $6,000 ÷ $15,000 = 40%. Growth comes from B and C, each tested properly with the kill and scale rules. Cutting a profitable partner to hit a percentage would be a mistake; growing the others is the fix.

rows: B: sports and casino, KE, hybrid

steps.say: Here's an example plan to bring concentration under forty percent. Notice the method: grow the others, don't cut the one that works. Operator A stays at six thousand dollars, but drops from sixty percent to forty, because the total grows. Operator B grows from three thousand to five thousand, and C from one thousand to four thousand, each tested with the kill and scale rules. Total goes from ten to fifteen thousand. Read the target column as a direction, not a deadline.

steps.p: Example: one buyer's portfolio. Two traffic sources feed three operators across three geos. No single line carries everything, so one failure slows the business without stopping it.
steps.say: This map shows an example portfolio for one buyer. Meta ads send sports traffic to three operators, in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana. A Telegram channel sends content traffic to two of them. Then operators A and C pay commission on C P A, and B on hybrid. Notice that no single line carries everything. So one failure slows the business, without stopping it.

steps.p: Run these steps before you send real volume to any new operator or network. Skipping them is how affiliates end up with unpaid invoices. They apply however good the payout looks.

steps.title: Verify the licence

steps.say: Run these steps before sending real volume to any new operator. Tap Next to follow each step. Second, get the terms in writing: payout, qualification, carryover, cap, payment terms and ad guidelines. Third, test tracking, with the postback tested end to end. Fourth, send a small capped test, for example twenty F T Ds, first-time deposits, and judge on qualified F T Ds. Fifth, scale only after the first invoice is paid in full and on time.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. They keep you diversified without spreading yourself too thin to test properly. Review them each quarter as your volume and partner list grow.

And if a partner pays late twice, freeze new volume to them. Review these each quarter as you grow.

lessons.title: Retention and player lifetime, done honestly
objectives: By the end you can explain what affiliates can and cannot do to support player retention.
By the end you can estimate the value of better retention on a RevShare or hybrid deal.
By the end you can run an opt-in content channel with responsible frequency rules.

steps.h: Why retention matters, and its limits
steps.p: On RevShare and hybrid deals, players who keep playing keep paying you. But the operator owns the player relationship and its marketing. Your role is limited to honest content people chose to receive, never pushing deposits or play.

d.s: Retention for affiliates is about useful content.

steps.say: On RevShare and hybrid deals, players who keep playing keep paying you. But the operator owns the player relationship and its marketing. Your role is limited to honest content that people chose to receive. You never push deposits or play. As the screen says, earn attention, never push play. For affiliates, retention is about useful content.

steps.h: What you can and cannot do
steps.p: The line is simple: you can give people useful, honest content they asked for. You cannot pressure them to deposit, chase losses or come back.

a.title: Not allowed or not honest
items: Messaging numbers you scraped or bought
Bonus pushes to people who left

b.title: Honest and allowed
items: Easy way to leave, and RG resources

steps.say: The line is simple. Compare the columns. Not allowed or not honest: messages like you haven't deposited in seven days, messaging numbers you scraped or bought, showing only winning tips, and bonus pushes to people who left. Honest and allowed: weekly fixture previews with an eighteen plus line, an opt-in channel people joined themselves, a full tip record including losses, and an easy way to leave, with responsible gambling resources.

steps.p: Example: share of a 100-player cohort still active each month. The community line represents players who also follow a useful content channel. Both decline; one declines more slowly.
steps.more: These are illustrative numbers, not a measured effect. Whether a channel improves retention for your players is something you test with cohorts, not something to assume.
steps.say: This curve shows an example of the share of a hundred-player cohort still active each month. The lower line has no community. The upper line represents players who also follow a useful content channel. Both decline, but one declines more slowly, thirty five percent at month six versus twenty eight. These are illustrative numbers, not a measured effect. Whether a channel helps your players is something you test with cohorts, not something to assume.

steps.h: Worked example: what retention is worth
steps.p: Example: in month 6, 35 players are active instead of 28. At $20 average monthly NGR per active player and 30% RevShare, that is a modest monthly gain that compounds over time.
steps.more: $42 a month from one cohort is small. Across twelve cohorts it becomes about $500 a month, if the effect holds. Weigh it against the time a channel takes to run. Never try to raise it by pushing play; the honest version is the only one worth having.
steps.say: What's that retention worth? In this example, in month six, thirty five players are active instead of twenty eight, so seven extra. At twenty dollars average monthly N G R, net gaming revenue, per active player, that's one hundred and forty dollars extra a month. Your thirty percent share is forty two dollars a month. It's modest, and it compounds over time if the effect holds. Never try to raise it by pushing play.

steps.p: Here is the kind of post that keeps an opt-in channel useful. It gives information, sets expectations and carries the age and responsible gambling message.

messages.text: Weekend preview: 3 fixtures, kickoff times in WAT, team news and form for each.
Last week's picks: 2 won, 3 lost. Full record pinned. Tips are opinions, not guarantees.
18+ only. Bet only what you can afford to lose. Set a deposit limit in your account settings.

Then last week's record: two won, three lost, with the full record pinned, and tips are opinions, not guarantees. Then the line: eighteen plus only, bet only what you can afford to lose, set a deposit limit. And notice the leave channel button.

steps.p: Retention also depends on the calendar. In years without a major tournament, the European football off-season leaves a quiet gap in June and July. Plan content and budget for it instead of forcing activity.
steps.say: Retention also depends on the calendar. Look at the table. During the European season, there are the most fixtures and interest, so run a full schedule. In the off-season, in years without a major tournament, June and July are quiet, with fewer fixtures, so cover other sports with a lower budget. In a tournament summer, national teams bring new bettors, so use the event plan from Module four. Plan for the quiet gap instead of forcing activity.

steps.p: These turn a useful channel into one that harms players and gets reported or removed. Each one has a simple fix, shown after the line.

Hiding losing tips|publish the full record
Messaging bought lists|opt-in members only
No way to leave|easy exit, removed on request
steps.say: These mistakes turn a useful channel into one that harms players and gets reported or removed. Look at each card and its fix. Daily bonus pushes: keep it mostly content, with rare offers. Hiding losing tips: publish the full record. Messaging bought lists: opt-in members only. And no way to leave: make exit easy, and remove people on request.

steps.p: Messaging people who did not opt in can break data protection and direct marketing laws, and platform rules. Gambling marketing to people who have asked to stop, or who have self-excluded, can also break gambling rules.

d.text: Send content only to people who opted in, honour every request to stop, and follow local data protection, direct marketing and gambling rules. Check them per geo.

steps.p: Players stay with a channel that respects them: accurate times, honest records, no hype and a clear way out. That trust is also what keeps your channel within the rules and the operator happy to work with you.

That same trust keeps your channel within the rules, and keeps the operator happy to work with you. As the screen says, earn the right to stay in their feed. Respect is the retention strategy.

By the end you can scale budget within caps using the scale rules and quality gate.

steps.h: Why negotiation is the cheapest growth
steps.p: A better deal on the same traffic raises profit without more spend or more risk. Operators raise payouts for affiliates who send steady, qualified, compliant volume and can prove it. Your weekly reviews from Module 5 are your negotiating file.
steps.say: A better deal on the same traffic raises profit without more spend or more risk. Operators raise payouts for affiliates who send steady, qualified, compliant volume, and can prove it. As the screen says, your data is your leverage. Your weekly reviews from Module five are your negotiating file.

steps.p: Bring evidence the operator can check against its own data. Managers need numbers to get a better deal approved internally. Pull it from your weekly scorecards.
d: Volume history|qualified FTDs per month, 3 months or more
Quality|qualified rate and redeposit rate by month
Player value|cohort NGR per player at 30 and 90 days
Compliance record|no flags, fast fixes, review log
Plan|the volume you can add if terms improve
steps.say: Bring evidence the operator can check against its own data. Look at the cards. Volume history, qualified F T Ds, first-time deposits, per month, for three months or more. Quality, your qualified rate and redeposit rate by month. Player value, cohort N G R, net gaming revenue, per player at thirty and ninety days. Your compliance record: no flags, fast fixes, a review log. And your plan, the volume you can add if terms improve. Managers need numbers to get a deal approved internally.

steps.p: Ask for one or two specific things, not everything at once. Each ask below has a clear value you can calculate before the conversation. Pick the one that matters most to your business right now.
d: Higher CPA|the most direct gain
Easier qualification|more of your FTDs paid
Hybrid or RevShare upgrade|long-term upside
No or reset carryover|protects against big wins
Higher cap|room to scale
Faster payment terms|better cash flow
steps.say: Ask for one or two specific things, not everything at once. Your options: a higher C P A, cost per acquisition, the most direct gain. Easier qualification, so more of your F T Ds are paid. A hybrid or RevShare upgrade, for long-term upside. No carryover or a reset, to protect against big wins. A higher cap, for room to scale. Or faster payment terms, for better cash flow. Each has a value you can calculate, so pick the one that matters most right now.

steps.h: Worked example: the value of the ask
steps.p: Example: you send 120 qualified FTDs a month at $40. Your 90-day cohort value is strong. You ask for $46, a 15% rise. Check both your gain and the operator's side.
steps.more: Showing the operator's side makes the ask easier to approve: at $46 they still earn $24 of NGR per player over six months before their own costs. If your cohort value were $45, a $46 ask would leave them losing money and you should not expect a yes. The data tells you what is realistic.
steps.say: Let's value an ask. In this example, you send a hundred and twenty qualified F T Ds a month at forty dollars, so forty eight hundred a month. You ask for forty six, a fifteen percent rise, which is fifty five twenty. Your gain is seven hundred and twenty dollars a month. Now the operator's side: six-month N G R per player is seventy dollars, so at forty six they keep twenty four per player. Showing that makes the ask easier to approve. If their value were forty five, don't expect a yes.

steps.p: Here is a short, specific negotiation. The affiliate leads with data, makes one clear ask, offers something in return and confirms in writing. Notice that the affiliate accepts a partial yes.

messages.text: Three months: 110, 118, 124 qualified FTDs. Qualified rate 74%. 90-day NGR per player $52. Report attached.
Could we move CPA from $40 to $46 and the cap to 160? We would add Kenya traffic next month.
I can do $44 now and review $46 at 150 a month. Cap 160 approved.
Agreed. Please confirm by email with the start date so we both have it in writing.

steps.say: Here's a negotiation done well. Notice the affiliate leads with data: three months of one ten, one eighteen and one twenty four qualified F T Ds, a seventy four percent qualified rate, and fifty two dollars of ninety-day N G R per player. Then one clear ask, forty six dollars and a cap of one sixty, with something offered in return, Kenya traffic. The manager offers forty four now, reviewing forty six at one fifty a month, and approves the cap. The affiliate accepts the partial yes, and asks for email confirmation.

steps.p: A short note from the founder on how to approach managers when asking for better terms. Use it as a reminder before every negotiation call.
steps.d: Walk in with three months of clean numbers and one clear ask. Managers can approve data. They cannot approve noise.

steps.p: Scale in this order. Each step depends on the one before it, and skipping a step is how scaling turns a profitable campaign into a loss.
d: Prove at target
Pass the quality gate
Confirm cap room
Scale +20% steps
Negotiate terms
Add geo or partner
steps.say: Scale in this order. Follow the flow. Prove the campaign at target. Pass the quality gate. Confirm you have room under the cap. Scale in plus twenty percent steps. Negotiate terms. Then add a geo or partner. Each step depends on the one before it. Skipping a step is how scaling turns a profitable campaign into a loss.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. These combine the foundations scale rule with the quality and cap checks from this school. Check all five before every budget step.
steps.more: Example: cap 160 FTDs a month. 80% is 128. If you are on track for 120 and a 20% budget step would add about 24 FTDs, you would reach about 144, over the 128 line, so ask for a higher cap before taking the step. FTDs above a cap may not be paid; check your terms.
d: Scale +20% every ≥ 48 hours at cost per qualified ≤ 0.8 × target with ≥ 3 qualified
Quality gate passed: qualified rate ≥ 60% of account average
Planned monthly FTDs ≤ 80% of the cap
Stop scaling if cost per qualified is above target in 2 reviews in a row
New partner: no scaling before the first full payment
steps.say: Here are starting scale rules to check before every budget step. Scale plus twenty percent every forty eight hours or more, at cost per qualified of point eight times target or less, with at least three qualified. The quality gate: qualified rate at least sixty percent of account average. Planned monthly F T Ds at or under eighty percent of the cap. Stop scaling if cost per qualified is above target in two reviews in a row. And with a new partner, no scaling before the first full payment. F T Ds above a cap may not be paid, so check your terms.

steps.h: Lab: daily budget for a monthly goal
steps.p: Use the budget lab to turn a monthly qualified FTD goal into a daily budget at your target cost per qualified FTD. Then read the explanation underneath.
steps.more: 150 × $30 = $4,500 for the month. $4,500 ÷ 30 = $150 a day. Reach it in +20% steps from where you are today, not in one jump, and only while the scale rules hold.

d.task: Goal 150 qualified FTDs in 30 days at a $30 target. What daily budget?

steps.say: Time for a lab. Your goal is one hundred and fifty qualified F T Ds in thirty days, at a thirty dollar target cost per qualified F T D. Use the budget lab to turn that monthly goal into a daily budget. Pause and try it, then check your answer. Then read the explanation underneath.

steps.p: Most of these mistakes come from impatience: asking without data, or scaling past what the deal will pay for. Each fix is slower in the moment and far cheaper over a quarter.

a.title: Mistake
items: Asking for more with one good week

b.title: Fix
items: Make one clear ask and offer something
Stay under 80% of cap or raise it first

steps.say: Most of these mistakes come from impatience. Asking for more after one good week. Threatening to move traffic. Accepting a verbal promise. Scaling past the cap. Jumping budget a hundred percent in a day. The fixes: bring three months of data, make one clear ask and offer something, confirm every change by email, stay under eighty percent of the cap or raise it first, and use plus twenty percent steps, forty eight hours apart.

steps.h: Compliance does not shrink at scale
steps.p: More volume means more ads, more creatives and more people seeing them. Every one still needs the pre-flight checks. Operators and regulators look harder at large affiliates, not less.

d.text: At scale, keep platform authorization, local law, age targeting and responsible gambling messaging on every ad. Get every deal change in writing. We are not certain this is current; check your contract and the operator's terms before relying on it.

steps.say: More volume means more ads, more creatives, and more people seeing them. Every one still needs the pre-flight checks, and operators and regulators look harder at large affiliates, not less. As the warning says, at scale keep platform authorization, local law, age targeting and responsible gambling messaging on every ad, and get every deal change in writing. We're not certain this is current, so check your contract and the operator's terms.

steps.h: Grow only what you can run responsibly
steps.p: Scale is only worth having if you can still review every creative, answer every flag within a day and keep your players' wellbeing in view. If the volume outgrows your review process, slow down until the process catches up.

d.b: Scale the process before the budget
d.s: If you cannot review it, do not run it.

quiz.q: You send 90 qualified FTDs a month at $35. You negotiate $40. Monthly gain?
Your cohort's 6-month NGR per player is $42. Is a CPA ask of $46 realistic?
options: Yes, CPA has nothing to do with NGR
Unlikely, it leaves the operator losing $4 per player before costs
quiz.why: The operator would pay more than it earns from your players.

quiz.q: Cap 100 FTDs a month. You are on track for 75. A 20% budget step would add about 15. What do you do?
options: Ask for a higher cap first
quiz.why: 75 + 15 = 90, above 80% of cap (80), so raise the cap first.

Assume it applies to last month
Ask them to confirm by email with the start date

lessons.say_intro: A better deal on the same traffic is the cheapest growth there is. In this lesson you'll prepare a data pack, make a specific ask to an affiliate manager, and scale budget safely within caps.
lessons.say_outro: To recap: negotiate with data and one clear ask, check the operator's side, and scale in steps within your cap and quality gate. Your task: prepare a one-page data pack for your best operator, with three months of qualified F T Ds, qualified rate, cohort value and compliance record, and write one specific ask with its value calculated. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: Stakes $80,000, winnings $73,000, bonuses $1,500, fees $500. RevShare 25%. Commission?
30% RevShare with carryover. M1 +$2,000, M2 −$4,000, M3 +$1,500, M4 +$3,500. Total paid over four months?
Same months without carryover. Total paid?
Offer A: 35% with a 20% admin fee. Offer B: 30%, no fee. On $10,000 GGR after bonuses, which pays more?
100 players cost $3,000. Hybrid $20 + 20%. Cumulative cohort NGR by month 4 is $5,100. Has the cohort paid back?
6-month value $90 per player, RevShare 35%, CPA $30. Does the rule allow moving volume to RevShare?
Total commission $12,000; largest partner $7,200. Concentration, and the action?
options: 60%; grow other partners toward a 40% cap
exam.why: $7,200 ÷ $12,000 = 60%. Grow the others rather than cutting a working partner.

exam.q: Cap 150. On track for 115. A +20% step adds about 23 FTDs. What do you do?
options: Ask for a higher cap first
exam.why: 115 + 23 = 138, above 80% of cap (120). Raise the cap first.

exam.q: Which channel practice is acceptable for retention?
options: Bonus messages to players who stopped depositing
Weekly opt-in previews with the full tip record and an 18+ RG line

exam.q: 120 qualified FTDs a month at $40; you ask for $45. Your cohort's 6-month NGR per player is $65. Gain to you and the operator's margin per player at $45?
exam.why: 120 × $5 = $600 a month. $65 − $45 = $20 per player before the operator's costs.
